title: Disorder-enhanced compressibility of Floquet random quantum circuits
authors: Francesca De Franco, Dante M. Kennes, David J. Luitz, Matteo Rizzi, Markus Schmitt
abstract: Current quantum hardware is limited by noise and decoherence, which restrict the depth of unitary circuits that can be implemented with high fidelity. We investigate how the compressibility of time-evolution operators depends on the dynamical regime of the underlying many-body system. As a testbed, we study a one-dimensional Floquet random circuit with a tunable competition between interactions and on-site disorder. Using tensor-network simulations, we characterize operator growth through the operator-entanglement entropy of the Floquet unitary as well as of out-of-time-ordered correlators (OTOCs). We find rapid operator scrambling at weak disorder, while strong disorder leads to slow OTOC-front propagation and logarithmic or near-logarithmic operator-entanglement growth over the accessible time window. We then optimize shallow brickwall circuits to approximate the Floquet evolution and show that strong-disorder circuits can be compressed to substantially smaller depths than weak-disorder circuits at fixed logarithmic fidelity density. These results suggest that localized or slowly scrambling dynamics provide a favorable regime for compressed quantum simulation on noisy devices.
summary: This paper analyzes Floquet random circuits to understand how system disorder affects the complexity and scrambling of quantum information. By measuring operator entanglement and correlators, the authors find that strong disorder slows down dynamics, enabling significant compression of required quantum circuit depths compared to weakly disordered systems. This suggests localized or slowly evolving dynamics are favorable for building reliable quantum simulators on noisy hardware.
main_problem: The study investigates how the compressibility of time-evolution operators changes based on the dynamical regime of a many-body system, particularly concerning noise limitations in quantum hardware.
main_result: Strong disorder regimes lead to slow operator scrambling and allow for circuit compression to substantially smaller depths compared to weak disorder circuits at fixed fidelity levels.
method: The research employs tensor-network simulations (TEBD) to calculate key diagnostics like Operator Entanglement Entropy (OPEE) and Out-of-Time Ordered Correlators (OTOCs), followed by variational circuit compression optimization.
model_or_system: The testbed is a one-dimensional Floquet random quantum circuit, which models dynamics with tunable competition between local disorder (random rotations) and interactions via two-qubit gates.
key_observables: Operator Entanglement Entropy (OPEE), Out-of-Time Ordered Correlators (OTOCs), and the minimal required circuit depth ($\langle D_{\min} angle$).
important_parameters: Disorder strength ($\alpha$), system size ($N$), and fidelity threshold ($f$). The regimes studied include weak vs. strong disorder, correlating with MBL physics.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on tensor-network approximations (e.g., truncation error set to $10^{-7}$) for simulating the time evolution of complex operators.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate OPEE and bond dimension growth curves showing transitions between power-law and logarithmic scaling based on disorder strength, alongside t-SNE plots visualizing structured gate distributions at high disorder.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the Floquet random circuit model, analyzes dynamics using OPEE/OTOCs to characterize scrambling regimes (weak vs. strong disorder), and finally optimizes shallow brickwall circuits to demonstrate compression benefits in the strongly disordered case.
why_interesting: It directly connects concepts from condensed matter physics (MBL, disorder) with practical quantum computing limitations (noise, circuit depth), suggesting a physical mechanism for robust quantum simulation.
